content:
A theory about how former Apple employees could retain access to confidential files after leaving for OpenAI has been debunked by court documents.

It was speculated that the file access may have involved accidental access due to a messy iCloud arrangement for Apple employees, but Apple says this is not the case...

事件簡述

Apple last month filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the company of stealing trade secrets related to hardware projects. One focal point of the allegations involves a former Apple employee named Chang Liu, who subsequently joined OpenAI. Here is a brief timeline of events:

  • July 10: Apple sues OpenAI, alleging that former Apple employees systematically stole Apple trade secrets to benefit future OpenAI hardware projects
  • July 10: OpenAI issues a brief denial in response
  • July 14: OpenAI files an updated response stating it has seen no evidence to support Apple's allegations.
  • August 3: OpenAI publishes a blog post blasting Apple's lawsuit
  • August 4: Apple moves for an injunction to prevent "irreparable harm"

iCloud 亂局

OpenAI says a flaw in Apple's information security left former employees with "unexpected" continued access to confidential files after their departure.

Earlier this week, The Information published a report suggesting that OpenAI was referring to a messy iCloud situation.

The report indicated that while Apple revokes former employees' access to company-managed iCloud folders, many files may have already been shared to Apple employees' personal accounts, and these employees may not only retain access to such files after leaving but could also continue to receive push updates.

In other words, former employees may receive push updates of confidential documents on their personal devices without any wrongdoing on their part.

Apple 表示此說法與事實不符

However, John Gruber of Daring Fireball pointed out that Apple stated explicitly in its court filings that the documents in question were not stored in iCloud.

Gruber believes these documents were very likely stored on Box, a cloud storage service that has long been widely used internally at Apple.

9to5Mac 觀點

For now, everything remains at a stage where each side sticks to its own version of events. We still have to wait for the case to be adjudicated to separate fact from fiction.

However, this messy iCloud arrangement appears to have been tacitly acknowledged by Apple. The arrangement seemingly aims to prevent Apple employees from having to carry both a personal and a corporate iPhone, which is understandable, but does indeed seem to constitute a significant security loophole.
